title: Cross-Lab Safety Eval Disagreement: When Different Public Evals Rank the Same Models Differently

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Lab Safety Eval Disagreement: When Different Public Evals Rank the Same Models Differently

**Problem:** Different public safety evaluations claim to measure overlapping constructs (e.g. 'harmlessness', 'jailbreak robustness'), yet may rank the same models in conflicting orders — a failure mode that undermines any governance regime relying on 'pass an eval'. The degree of cross-eval disagreement is not well characterized for governance audiences.

**Direction:** Characterize eval disagreement. Select 4-6 small open models and 3-4 distinct public safety evals targeting similar constructs. Run all evals on all models on a single GPU, then compute rank correlations between evals. Identify pairs of evals that disagree and inspect example items to explain why (different harm taxonomies, scoring, prompt styles). Report whether 'the model is safe' is eval-dependent.

**Why it matters:** International consensus on evaluation methodology is an explicit open problem (INAISI). Demonstrating that current evals disagree on rankings is direct evidence that a single eval can't anchor governance decisions and that standardization is needed. Small open models, public evals, single GPU — independent and reproducible.

**Relevant context:** INAISI consensus-methodology open problem; Safetywashing on benchmark correlations; Safety Under Scaffolding on condition-dependence.

title: Distillation as a Threshold Bypass: Can a Tiny Student Inherit Regulated Capability From a Big Teacher?

# Distillation as a Threshold Bypass: Can a Tiny Student Inherit Regulated Capability From a Big Teacher?

**Problem:** Model reuse via distillation is named as a compute-threshold loophole: a small, sub-threshold student model can inherit much of a large teacher's capability, escaping systemic-risk obligations. The boundary — how much regulated capability transfers cheaply — is rarely demonstrated concretely for governance readers.

**Direction:** Probe the distillation-transfer boundary on a feasible slice. Using an existing open small model and a larger open teacher (or public teacher-generated outputs), do a lightweight distillation-style fine-tune on a single GPU for one narrow capability, and measure how much of the teacher's performance the tiny student captures per unit of (sub-threshold) compute. Frame results as 'effective regulated capability acquired below the threshold'. (Scope: small models only, short runs, no from-scratch training.)

**Why it matters:** It concretely shows regulators that training-compute thresholds can be sidestepped by reuse, supporting the case for capability- or behavior-based triggers. Uses only small open models and short single-GPU fine-tunes — within beginner reach and fully counterfactual to lab work. Marked lower-confidence due to the light fine-tuning component.

**Relevant context:** Compute-threshold loophole taxonomy (fine-tuning, distillation, model expansion, inference scaling) in arXiv 2502.00003; DeepSeek-R1 efficiency result; EU/US thresholds.

title: Promise vs Practice in Watermarking: Does AI-Content Transparency Survive Trivial Edits?

# Promise vs Practice in Watermarking: Does AI-Content Transparency Survive Trivial Edits?

**Problem:** The EU Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content leans on labeling/watermarking commitments. A known failure mode is that detectable provenance signals (watermarks, metadata) are fragile to trivial transformations (paraphrase, screenshot, re-encode), making the transparency commitment hollow. The robustness of available open watermarking/detection to simple edits is undercharacterized for policy audiences.

**Direction:** Stress-test provenance robustness as the failure mode. Using an open text watermarking scheme (or open AI-text detectors) on a single GPU, generate watermarked/AI text, then apply simple, realistic edits (paraphrasing with a small model, synonym swaps, truncation, format changes) and measure detection survival. Report the edit budget at which transparency signals break and characterize which edits defeat them most cheaply.

**Why it matters:** Transparency-of-AI-content rules assume provenance signals persist; if a screenshot or paraphrase erases them, the regulation can't achieve its goal. Quantifying fragility gives the EU AI Office concrete evidence on what to require. Open tools, small models, single GPU — independent and policy-relevant.

**Relevant context:** EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content; watermark-robustness and AI-text-detection literature; transparency obligations under EU AI Act Article 50.

title: Who Audits the Auditors: Mapping Conflict-of-Interest Structures in the Emerging AI Audit Market

# Who Audits the Auditors: Mapping Conflict-of-Interest Structures in the Emerging AI Audit Market

**Problem:** Audit-washing arises when second-party auditors cater to paying clients and first-party audits internalize the auditee's interests. As a commercial AI-audit market emerges, the structural conflict-of-interest patterns (who pays, who selects scope, who can publish negative findings) are not systematically mapped — a governance failure mode hiding in plain sight.

**Direction:** Characterize conflict structures across the audit ecosystem. Compile a sample of organizations offering AI audits/assurance and code each on independence dimensions: funding source (paid by auditee vs not), scope control, publication rights, certification incentives, and revolving-door ties. Build a simple taxonomy of conflict configurations and quantify how many actors sit in high-conflict arrangements. Compare against safeguards from mature audit professions (financial, safety-critical).

**Why it matters:** Third-party audit is the proposed backbone of AI accountability, but it fails silently if incentives are misaligned. A structural map gives policymakers the evidence to mandate independence safeguards before the market ossifies. Pure desk research on public information — no compute, classic independent governance scholarship.

**Relevant context:** Outsider Oversight (arXiv 2206.04737); GMF 'AI Audit-Washing and Accountability'; TechPolicy.Press on mandated third-party audits; CCG blog on audit access/roadblocks.

**Why it matters:** International coordination on AI governance is impossible if the foundational definitions don't align. A precise drift map is directly actionable for harmonization efforts (INAISI, treaty design) and shows where a model can fall through every net. Pure document analysis — no model, no compute, classic independent policy work.

title: The Red-Teaming Black Box: Do Published Safety Reports Disclose Enough to Trust Their Red-Team Claims?

# The Red-Teaming Black Box: Do Published Safety Reports Disclose Enough to Trust Their Red-Team Claims?

**Problem:** Seoul commitments and frontier frameworks promise internal and external red-teaming, and labs cite red-teaming as evidence of safety. But a failure mode is that red-team disclosures omit the information needed to assess rigor (who, how many prompts, what coverage, what was found and fixed), making the claim unfalsifiable. The disclosure quality has not been systematically scored.

**Direction:** Score red-teaming disclosure quality. Build a rubric of what a credible red-team report should disclose (independence of red-teamers, methodology, scope/coverage, quantitative findings, remediation, residual risk). Apply it to the publicly available safety reports/system cards of ~8-12 recent model releases and grade each. Identify the systematically-omitted elements and which labs disclose most/least.

**Why it matters:** Red-teaming is a headline pillar of voluntary commitments and emerging regulation; if reports are too opaque to evaluate, the pillar is decorative. A disclosure scorecard tells regulators exactly what to require for red-teaming to be auditable — the third-party-verification open problem. Public reports only, no compute, independent.

**Relevant context:** Seoul commitments (red-teaming + info sharing); METR common elements; AI Transparency Atlas disclosure deficits; Outsider Oversight on audit access.

title: Stale by Design: Measuring How Fast Fixed Compute Thresholds Decay Against the Efficiency Frontier

# Stale by Design: Measuring How Fast Fixed Compute Thresholds Decay Against the Efficiency Frontier

**Problem:** A structural failure mode of compute-threshold governance is that a fixed FLOP line becomes increasingly permissive as algorithmic efficiency improves — last year's frontier capability is reachable below threshold today. The decay rate of threshold effectiveness has not been empirically estimated from public capability/compute trends for a policy audience.

**Direction:** Estimate the threshold-decay rate. Using Epoch AI compute and capability data, fit the trend of 'compute needed to reach a fixed capability level' over time. Project how a static 10^25 threshold's coverage of frontier-equivalent capability shrinks year over year, and estimate the doubling time of the threshold's permissiveness. Translate into 'how often a fixed threshold would need to be lowered to hold capability coverage constant'.

**Why it matters:** It quantifies, for compute-governance designers, exactly how badly fixed thresholds erode and how aggressively they'd need indexing to stay meaningful — directly informing dynamic-threshold design (Epoch AI, MIRI agenda). Uses only public Epoch trend data and basic regression — beginner statistics, no compute, fully counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Context note that fixed thresholds become permissive as efficiency advances; Epoch AI compute tracking; DeepSeek-R1 efficiency result; compute-threshold limitation analyses.
